quiz.text: Both options exist, but which approach do we recommend for how 44i Digital is introduced?
options: Complete white label, so the client never hears our name
Naming us openly as your digital partner
Deciding case by case, per client
Avoiding the subject unless asked
quiz.why: Both exist, but we lean toward naming us openly as your digital partner — it is cleaner and makes everything easier from day one.

quiz.text: Who helps with the agency name, the web address, and the website?
options: You hire a local designer
We do — twenty-five years of marketing experience, and we build the site
It is handled after your first sale
Each group is on its own
quiz.why: You are not doing it by yourself — we help you land on a name, find an available web address, and build the site.

quiz.text: A client asks who actually does the digital work. What should happen?
options: Change the subject and follow up later
Answer differently depending on the client
Say it depends on the service
Give the answer your group already decided on, the same way every time
quiz.why: Pick one answer, write it down, and make sure everyone gives it the same way every time.

quiz.text: What is the practical advice on choosing a name?
options: Make it as descriptive as possible
Match your parent brand exactly
Say your shortlist out loud — you will be saying it several times a day for years
Prioritise the tagline over the name
quiz.why: Do not overthink the tagline. Say the name out loud — if it is hard to say on the phone, pick another.

quiz.text: Where do the logo files, social graphics, and display ads for your new agency live?
options: You commission them from a local designer
Behind the owners and operators login on your resource site
They are sent after your first sale
Each group creates its own
quiz.why: A lot of it is already made for you — behind the owners and operators login on your resource site.

quiz.text: Which tool helps you model what recurring digital revenue looks like for your business?
options: The CPC/CPM calculator
The client reports folder
The hosting and website revenue calculator
The Trello board
quiz.why: The hosting and website revenue calculator lets you model recurring digital revenue before you decide how big to go.

quiz.text: Why is it worse for two people in your office to give different answers than to be vague?
options: It takes longer to correct
The client starts wondering what else is unclear
It breaches the partnership agreement
It slows down onboarding
quiz.why: A client who hears two versions starts questioning everything else — write it down and circulate it.

quiz.text: A group is about to commission a logo and a set of social graphics. What should they do first?
options: Get three quotes
Check the owners and operators login — much of it already exists
Wait until after the client announcement
Design it in-house to save money
quiz.why: Building the brand from scratch wastes money and weeks — much of it already exists behind the login. Ask first.

quiz.text: Why does controlling the digital budget matter to your business?
options: Digital is cheaper to fulfill
Traditional budgets are moving, and that money goes either through you or around you
It reduces the number of clients you need
It replaces traditional services entirely
quiz.why: That money is not disappearing — the only question is whether it goes through you or around you.

quiz.text: What comes immediately after this block?
options: Submitting your first insertion order
Getting ready to sell — your own house, your team’s training, and telling your clients
Building your client reports
The digital audit tool
quiz.why: Next is Getting Ready to Sell — your own house, your team’s training, and telling your clients.

quiz.text: What does every group receive automatically at onboarding?
options: A social media management program
A Google Business Profile audit
A website that we build for them
A set of targeted landing pages
quiz.why: Every group gets a website — we build it, you don’t lift a finger. It’s the first thing that happens.

quiz.text: What happens with the blog program?
options: You write it and we post it
We write it every other week, post it on your site, and you can email it to your database
We write it quarterly for an additional fee
It is available only as a paid add-on
quiz.why: We write a blog every other week and post it — so your site never looks abandoned and you always have something to email.

quiz.text: What percentage of your client base should be told about the new agency?
options: The top twenty percent
Whoever asks
One hundred percent
Only clients currently buying digital
quiz.why: Tell every single client — the one you assume isn’t interested is often the one quietly paying somebody else.

quiz.text: What are the two ways your team gets trained?
options: A written manual and an annual conference
Guided certification with weekly account-manager meetings, plus Wednesday sales training on Zoom
On-site visits twice a year
Self-paced video only, with no support
quiz.why: Certification with your account manager weekly makes you competent; Wednesdays keep you sharp. Do both.

quiz.text: Where are the one-sheets and the presentation deck, already branded to your group?
options: You build them yourself
In Client Forms on your resource site
They are emailed monthly
Behind the owners and operators login
quiz.why: Client Forms holds a one-sheet for every tactic plus a deck already branded to your group — you’re not making slides.

quiz.text: What is the easiest way to get digital into every pitch?
options: Add a pricing page at the back
Mention it verbally during the meeting
Include the Digital House graphic in the presentation
Send a follow-up email afterward
quiz.why: The Digital House graphic shows a client everything you can do on one page — you’re selling a whole house.

quiz.text: Why is announcing before training a mistake?
options: Announcements require approval first
A curious client asks a reasonable question and nobody can answer it
The resource site is not available yet
Clients expect a formal launch event
quiz.why: A blank look turns the launch into a press release instead of a business. Train first, announce second.

quiz.text: Where should digital sit in a proposal?
options: On the last page, as an optional add-on
In a separate document
In the middle, where the conversation happens
Only if the client asks about it
quiz.why: If it’s the last page, it’s the first thing cut. Put it in the middle where the conversation happens.

quiz.text: Why does the order matter — house and training before the announcement?
options: The resource site unlocks in stages
An announcement nobody can back up quietly becomes a press release instead of a business
Client contracts require it
Training is only offered before launch
quiz.why: Ready, then announce — an announcement nobody can stand behind goes quiet.

quiz.text: What comes immediately after this block?
options: Your first insertion order
Your resource section, where everything you sell actually lives
Client reporting
The digital audit tool
quiz.why: Next is your resource section — where every form, tool, presentation, and report lives.

quiz.text: When you accept your Trello invitation, what has to match?
options: Your group name
The email address the invitation was sent to
Your Trello handle from the insertion order
Your manager’s login
quiz.why: Sign up with the same email the invitation was sent to, or you get an account that cannot see your board.

quiz.text: What is the first setting you should change?
options: Board background color
Card sorting order
Email notifications, from periodic to instantly
Your display name
quiz.why: Periodic batching means you find out Thursday about a Tuesday question — switch to instantly.

quiz.text: Where do you post a question that is not about a specific client?
options: On any client’s card
In General Questions, tagging somebody
By email to your account manager
In Quick Resources
quiz.why: General Questions is for anything not tied to a client — use the handle so the right people are notified.

quiz.text: On a client’s list, how do you tell what stage something is at?
options: The card’s position in the list
The date it was created
The labels — live, on hold, complete
You have to ask
quiz.why: Labels tell you the status at a glance — live, on hold, complete.

quiz.text: What can you do with a Trello email notification besides read it?
options: Forward it to fulfillment
Reply to it — your reply lands on the right card automatically
Print it for the client file
Nothing, it is read-only
quiz.why: Reply straight to the email and it lands on the right card — no logging in and hunting.

quiz.text: Where would you find service timelines and ad specifications?
options: The Recommendations section
Your client’s card
Quick Resources
The resource site only
quiz.why: Quick Resources holds training links, contact routing, service timelines, and ad specs.

quiz.text: You move a card to a different position on the board. What happens?
options: Nothing — position is cosmetic
It drops out of the queue our team works from, and the campaign quietly stops progressing
The client is notified of the change
Fulfillment is prompted to re-prioritise it
quiz.why: The position is doing a job — move a card and it leaves the working queue, and progress stalls silently.

quiz.text: You post a comment on a card but do not tag anybody. What is the result?
options: It is deleted after seven days
Everyone on the board is notified
Nobody is notified, so your question sits there unread
It becomes visible only to you
quiz.why: A comment with no @ tag is a note nobody gets told about — it just sits there looking handled.

quiz.text: Why should conversations happen on the card rather than by email?
options: Email is not permitted under the partnership agreement
A comment is visible to whoever picks it up, and it stays as the record
Trello sends faster notifications than email
Email cannot include attachments
quiz.why: A card comment is visible to whoever picks it up and becomes the record; an email reaches one person who may be out.

quiz.text: What comes immediately after this block?
options: Submitting your first insertion order
MRR prospect research — deciding whether a business is worth your time
Client reporting
Intake form training
quiz.why: Next is MRR prospect research — whether a business is worth your time before you pick up the phone.

quiz.text: How are the top-level folders organized?
options: Alphabetically
By the three steps of a sale
By product category
By date added
quiz.why: Not alphabetically — by the sale. Step one, step two, step three are the three stages of every deal.

quiz.text: Your password stops working. What is the most likely reason?
options: The site is down
Your account was removed
Passwords change every ninety days
You need to request access again
quiz.why: It is case-sensitive and rotates every ninety days — your manager or owner has the current one.

quiz.text: What are the two ways to sell described in step one?
options: Phone or in person
New business or existing clients
Pitching directly, or requesting a recommendation from our strategy team
Monthly or annual agreements
quiz.why: Pitch it directly after the needs analysis, or send it to our strategy team for a tailored recommendation.

quiz.text: What are “packages”?
options: Printed materials mailed to clients
Pre-built bundles of tactics that work well together
Pricing tiers for each product
A folder of past proposals
quiz.why: Pre-built tactic bundles — start from one that already makes sense and tailor it.

quiz.text: Where is the presentation material for client meetings?
options: You create it yourself
In the Reports section
In Client Forms, already branded to your group
It is emailed monthly
quiz.why: Client Forms holds one-sheets for every tactic plus a deck already branded to your group.

quiz.text: The needs analysis appears in both step one and step two. Why?
options: It is a duplicate that has not been cleaned up
Step one holds the blank form; step two is where the completed one goes back in with the recommendation request
Step one is for new clients and step two is for existing ones
Step two’s version is a different form entirely
quiz.why: Same document, two moments — blank form picked up in step one, completed form returned in step two.

quiz.text: You saved a presentation deck to your desktop months ago. What is the risk?
options: The file will have expired
Materials get updated, so your copy is out of date
It will not open on a different computer
Client names are locked in
quiz.why: A deck saved eight months ago is eight months old — pull a fresh copy each time.

quiz.text: Why should you scroll past the three steps?
options: The steps do not work until the page fully loads
The podcast, featured training, calculator, and case studies all sit below them
Folders are reorganized monthly
Reports are only available at the bottom
quiz.why: All the below-the-fold content — podcast, training, calculator, case studies — lives under the three steps.

quiz.text: What is the main reason to learn what is in here before you start selling?
options: It is required to get a password
So you stop building things you already own, and stop improvising in front of clients
To choose which market you work in
To set your own pricing
quiz.why: When you know what is in there, you stop rebuilding finished materials and stop guessing in meetings.

quiz.text: Everything in this section feeds into which system for communication with our team?
options: Email
The insertion order form
Trello
The Digital Blueprint
quiz.why: Questions, orders, and campaign updates all happen on your Trello board — the next block.

quiz.text: What does a thin needs analysis actually break?
options: The insertion order
The audit — it ends up measuring against guessed keywords
The client’s Trello card
The reporting schedule
quiz.why: The profit centers you capture become the keywords the audit runs on — leave them thin and the audit measures against guesses.

quiz.text: How should the meeting open?
options: With a summary of your services
By telling them you are not selling today and explaining why you are asking questions
By reading the first section of the form
With the findings from your prospect research
quiz.why: Take selling off the table and they relax and answer honestly.

quiz.text: What is the best way to ask about profit centers?
options: Ask for a revenue breakdown by product line
Skip it and estimate from their website
Ask what makes them the most money — not what they sell the most of
Request their financial statements
quiz.why: Separating margin from volume gets a far better answer than “we do a bit of everything.”

quiz.text: A client hesitates on the share-of-sales question. What defuses it?
options: Move on and come back next meeting
Explain that the strategy team requires exact figures
Offer to sign a confidentiality agreement
“Rough thirds is fine — I’m not after your books, I just need to know where to point the advertising”
quiz.why: You’re not asking for financials — you’re asking where to aim.

quiz.text: What must you confirm before you leave?
options: The contract start date
The date you are presenting back to them
Their approval of a budget figure
Which services they want
quiz.why: It gives the team a deadline and gives you a reason to return.

quiz.text: Where is the blank needs analysis form?
options: Step two of the resource site
Step one of the resource site
Inside the online insertion order
On the Trello board
quiz.why: Picked up in step one, returned completed in step two.

quiz.text: Where does the completed form go?
options: Emailed to your account manager
Step two, together with your request for a recommendation
Step three, with the insertion order
Uploaded to the client’s Trello card
quiz.why: The completed CNA and the recommendation request go in together.

quiz.text: Why is skipping the money questions the most damaging mistake?
options: The form cannot be submitted without them
Profit centers become the keywords the digital audit runs on
Budget determines which services are available
The strategy team will not accept the submission
quiz.why: Skip them and you’ve quietly broken the next two steps.

quiz.text: How often should an existing client get a fresh needs analysis?
options: Only if they ask
Every time a campaign renews
At least once a year
Only when adding a new service
quiz.why: Businesses change, and it’s the easiest reason to be back in a room with a happy client.

quiz.text: What comes immediately after this block in the process?
options: The insertion order
The digital audit, which runs on the keywords you just captured
Client reporting
Requesting a recommendation
quiz.why: The profit centers you captured are exactly what the audit measures against.

quiz.text: What two things must be in place before an RFR will be built?
options: A signed insertion order and a start date
A completed needs analysis and a client-provided budget
A digital audit and a proposal
Manager approval and a credit check
quiz.why: Both come out of the same conversation — get both while you’re in the room.

quiz.text: Why does a generic recommendation get declined?
options: It usually costs more
It wastes the research and conversation that made you credible
Clients are required to compare bids
It cannot be submitted as an insertion order
quiz.why: You did the work precisely so the plan would fit — a generic one throws that away.

quiz.text: In this business, how does an RFR differ from what the industry usually calls an RFP?
options: They are the same thing
An RFP is for existing clients only
An RFP is usually a client asking vendors to bid; an RFR is you asking your own team
An RFP includes pricing and an RFR does not
quiz.why: Same three letters, opposite direction — here you’re the one asking.

quiz.text: Which three things make an RFR mandatory?
options: Any campaign over a set budget, any new client, any website
An e-commerce site, a custom website, or a fully custom campaign
Social media, email, and search campaigns
Any deal involving more than three services
quiz.why: Those builds have moving parts that need scoping properly.

quiz.text: You do not have a budget figure from the client. What should you do?
options: Enter a figure that feels about right
Leave the field blank
Write “to be confirmed” and submit anyway
Go back to the client and get it — the RFR will not be built without it
quiz.why: There’s no “unknown” path; the next step is a phone call, not a submission.

quiz.text: The recommendation comes back and you disagree with part of it. What do you do?
options: Present it as written — the strategy team decided
Rebuild it yourself without telling anybody
Ask for the change on the Trello card
Submit a second RFR
quiz.why: A recommendation is a recommendation, not an instruction — you were in the room.

quiz.text: Where is the RFR submitted?
options: Step one of the resource site
Step two, together with the completed needs analysis
Step three, with the insertion order
Directly on the Trello board
quiz.why: It goes in with the CNA because they belong together.

quiz.text: Where does the request appear once submitted?
options: In your active client list
In the recommendations column on Trello
In Quick Resources
In the Reports section
quiz.why: It stays there until the deal is sold or shelved.

quiz.text: Your presentation is Thursday. When should the RFR go in?
options: Wednesday afternoon is fine
At least two business days beforehand, and earlier if possible
The same morning, marked urgent
Any time before the meeting
quiz.why: Two business days is a minimum for a reason — a rush job is a worse plan.

quiz.text: A rep submits an RFR without having run a needs analysis. What happens?
options: The strategy team builds a general plan instead
It comes back asking for the needs analysis, costing days
It is built using the digital audit alone
The account manager completes the needs analysis for them
quiz.why: The team won’t build a plan for a business nobody has spoken to.

quiz.text: Why does bringing this audit change the meeting?
options: It is faster than a normal sales call
It is proprietary — a competitor calling on that business cannot bring one
It replaces the need for a needs analysis
It sets the client’s budget
quiz.why: You arrive with a diagnosis; they arrive with a brochure and a price.

quiz.text: Why is the audit never printed, when the monthly report is?
options: Printing costs are not covered
The audit is our proprietary method — a printed copy can end up with a competitor
The audit is too long to print usefully
Clients prefer to view digitally
quiz.why: The report is proof of what they bought; the audit is how we find things — it stays with us.

quiz.text: Where should the business name, address, and website come from?
options: Typed from memory or from your notes
Copied exactly from their Google Business Profile
Whatever appears on their invoice
The needs analysis form
quiz.why: Consistency is what’s being measured — a slightly different version audits a business that doesn’t exist.

quiz.text: What do the four profit centers become in the audit?
options: The service categories that get scored
The search terms the business is measured against
The client’s budget allocation
The list of recommended products
quiz.why: Specificity is everything — “metal roofing,” not “general contracting.”

quiz.text: How should deficiencies be presented?
options: All of them at once, so the client sees the full picture
One at a time — prove it, explain what it costs, offer the fix, then stop
Ranked by score, highest to lowest
In writing only, so the client can review
quiz.why: Two per meeting is plenty; five is a list of everything wrong with somebody’s life’s work.

quiz.text: How should the walkthrough open?
options: With the biggest problem, for impact
With the overall summary
With something the business is doing well
With your recommendation
quiz.why: It costs thirty seconds and means the meeting isn’t a list of failures.

quiz.text: What is your source of truth for the business details?
options: Their website footer
Their Google Business Profile
The insertion order
The Trello card
quiz.why: Copy from it, never retype.

quiz.text: What do you do with the audit’s numbers?
options: Lead the meeting with them
Put them on the printed summary
Keep them — they help you find deficiencies, but a number reads as a grade
Compare them to industry averages for the client
quiz.why: A person who feels graded stops listening — show the finding, not the score.

quiz.text: A rep types a slightly different version of the business name. What breaks?
options: The audit will not generate
The listings result is meaningless, because consistency is what is measured
The social media scores are excluded
The client’s profile is edited
quiz.why: You’ve audited a business that doesn’t quite exist.

quiz.text: How is the audit presented to a client?
options: Printed and left with them for review
Emailed as a PDF ahead of the meeting
Live on a laptop or iPad, and never left behind
Posted to their Trello card
quiz.why: Turn the laptop around and scroll through it together.

quiz.text: Why can’t fulfillment begin before the IO is submitted?
options: Billing has to run first
The account manager has to approve the sale
Until the IO exists, there is no record of what was sold
Trello boards are built weekly
quiz.why: Nothing happens until the IO exists.

quiz.text: In step one, what happens when you select your name from the “I am” dropdown?
options: It emails your manager for approval
It fills in your Trello handle automatically
It locks the form to your account only
It skips you to step two
quiz.why: Not in the list yet? Just type your information in instead.

quiz.text: You are sitting with a client and you have an iPad. What is the preferred way to get the signature?
options: Email the form and wait for them to sign later
Type your own name on their behalf
Hand them the tablet and have them draw their signature
Print the review screen and have them sign the paper
quiz.why: A signature you get in the room is a signature; a form you email is a maybe.

quiz.text: A kick-off call is required. Why can’t you just type in a date?
options: The form only accepts dates in the current month
Kick-off calls are scheduled by fulfillment
The date and time fields stay locked until you open the AM’s calendar
You can, as long as you confirm it later
quiz.why: A call on the form but not on a calendar is a call that doesn’t happen.

quiz.text: You hit an intake question you are unsure about. What are your options?
options: Guess, and correct it after launch
Email the blank form to the client
Delay the IO until you have everything
Leave it blank, or use the help button to bring the account manager in
quiz.why: A guess reads like a fact to whoever builds the campaign.

quiz.text: Which intake form is handled by the account manager rather than the AE?
options: Reputation management
The website intake form
Whichever one the AE is least confident about
All of them
quiz.why: Websites have too many moving parts — that one isn’t yours to fill in.

quiz.text: Where should an existing client’s business name be corrected?
options: In the business name field on the IO
By submitting a new IO with the right name
In client profiles in the admin portal
In a comment on the Trello card
quiz.why: Renaming on the IO creates a duplicate instead of updating them.

quiz.text: You pick a returning client, then change their business name on the form. What happens?
options: The existing client record updates
The form blocks you from continuing
A duplicate client and a duplicate Trello list get created
The account manager is asked to approve the change
quiz.why: Now there are two of the same client and nobody knows which is real.

quiz.text: Where does the Trello card come from after you submit?
options: You create it manually on your board
The form builds it automatically
The account manager builds it during the kick-off call
It appears after the campaign goes live
quiz.why: Submission creates the record, the card, and the notifications on its own.

quiz.text: After you submit, what is your job?
options: Email the account manager the details
Wait for a phone call from fulfillment
Submit a second copy for your own records
Watch the Trello card — that is where the team asks for anything they need
quiz.why: The card is where the record lives and where questions land.

quiz.text: Where do the intake forms live?
options: In a separate folder on the resource site
Inside the insertion order, attached to the services you selected
Emailed to you after submission
On the client’s Trello card
quiz.why: You’re already in there — nothing extra to go and find.

quiz.text: What are the intake forms actually for?
options: Confirming the client agreed to the terms
Giving our team the basic information needed to start building the campaign
Recording which rep sold the deal
Documenting the needs analysis
quiz.why: A handful of basic facts, not a test.

quiz.text: What are your three options for handling an intake form?
options: Complete it, delegate it to the client, or skip it
Complete it, fill in what you know, or ask your account manager for help
Complete it or postpone it
Complete it yourself or have the client complete it
quiz.why: All three are fine.

quiz.text: You leave some fields blank. What happens next?
options: The insertion order cannot be submitted
The campaign launches without that information
The system prompts you to book a kick-off call with your account manager
The account manager completes it without telling you
quiz.why: The gap becomes a fifteen-minute conversation, not your homework.

quiz.text: Which three products always include a kick-off call?
options: Search, display, and social ads
Website development, social media management, and email marketing
Reputation, listings, and search
Any product over a set budget
quiz.why: Those carry decisions a form can’t hold.

quiz.text: Where is the “need help” option?
options: On the Trello card
Inside the intake form itself
In the resource section
On the review and submit screen
quiz.why: Press it and somebody picks it up with you.

quiz.text: Who handles the website development intake with the client?
options: The account executive
The account manager
The client, on their own
Whoever books the kick-off call
quiz.why: That one isn’t yours to fill in at all.

quiz.text: You remember something relevant after submitting. Where does it go?
options: An email to fulfillment
A second insertion order
The Trello card
Nowhere — it is too late
quiz.why: Remembered it on the drive home? Put it on the card.

quiz.text: You are unsure of an answer. What should you do?
options: Enter your best guess so the field is complete
Leave it blank, or press the help button
Send the client the question by email
Delay submitting the insertion order
quiz.why: Blank is safe — blank triggers a conversation.

quiz.text: Why is guessing worse than leaving a field blank?
options: Guesses are flagged automatically
A guess reads as a fact and gets built into the campaign
Blank fields speed up approval
Guesses invalidate the insertion order
quiz.why: The only mistake here that really costs anything.

quiz.text: What is the report’s actual job in the meeting?
options: To explain every metric in detail
To show the campaign delivered what was promised
To justify next month’s budget
To prove digital outperformed other media
quiz.why: That’s the honest scope — the campaign ran and did what was sold.

quiz.text: When are reports for the previous month available?
options: The last day of the month
By the seventh
Within twenty-four hours of a request
Quarterly
quiz.why: Report ready by the seventh, meeting mid-month, a week to prepare.

quiz.text: A large client asks for a live dashboard. What do you do?
options: Tell them it is not available
Promise it, since there is no extra fee
Ask your account manager — it is case by case and only for the programmatic products
Offer it for any service if the budget is big enough
quiz.why: Don’t promise one — display, video, streaming, and audio only.

quiz.text: When should the report meeting be scheduled?
options: After the report arrives, whenever the client is free
As a standing appointment in the middle of every month
At the end of the quarter
Only when the client requests it
quiz.why: Same client, same slot — you’re not chasing anybody.

quiz.text: What should the report conversation open with?
options: The impressions total
The definitions page
How is business, how is traffic, how are sales
A review of next month’s budget
quiz.why: Those three questions, and then listening — that’s the meeting.

quiz.text: Which page shows tactics the client is not currently buying?
options: The title page
The overview and definitions page
The service pages
The other services page
quiz.why: A structured upsell, in person, every month.

quiz.text: A number in the report looks wrong. Where does that go?
options: An email to the account manager
The Trello card
A note in next month’s report
A phone call to fulfillment
quiz.why: On the card, not into an email nobody can find later.

quiz.text: A number looks short before your meeting. What should you do?
options: Skip the meeting that month
Explain it to the client as best you can on your own
Raise it on the Trello card before the meeting so we can tell you what is going on
Wait for the client to notice
quiz.why: Our strategists review campaigns daily so it doesn’t land in your lap.

quiz.text: Why does unexplained jargon matter?
options: It slows the meeting down
It makes the client feel lost, and people do not renew things that make them feel lost
It is against reporting standards
It confuses the account manager
quiz.why: Translate anything into words they’d use at their own dinner table.

quiz.text: What does the reporting conversation lead into?
options: The end of the engagement
A renewal conversation and a fresh needs analysis
A new insertion order for the same services
A billing review
quiz.why: Not the end of the line — the top of the next lap.

quiz.text: What belongs in tier one, the foundation?
options: Display and streaming campaigns
Reviews and email marketing
A fast, findable website plus the search and profile work that makes it visible
Social media posting
quiz.why: Tier one is being found and having a place that works — the website, SEO/AEO, the Google Business Profile, landing pages.

quiz.text: What is tier two, the walls, for?
options: Driving new traffic to the website
Keeping a customer once they have found the business
Measuring campaign performance
Building the website itself
quiz.why: Walls keep a customer once you have found them — reputation, listings, social, email.

quiz.text: Why does targeted digital work better once the first two tiers are in place?
options: The platforms charge less for established businesses
Campaigns can run longer
There is finally somewhere worth sending people
It qualifies for better placements
quiz.why: The roof finally pays for itself because there is something underneath to send people to.

quiz.text: “Foundation-up” means…
options: Selling the largest product first
Building in sequence, starting with visibility
Starting with whichever tactic the client asks about
Beginning every campaign in a new quarter
quiz.why: Foundation-up is building in order, starting with visibility — the opposite of roof-down.

quiz.text: A “deficiency” is…
options: A tactic the client has not bought yet
A budget shortfall
A specific, provable gap in their online presence
A missing field on the needs analysis
quiz.why: A deficiency is a provable gap — a slow load time, a wrong number, four reviews — not an opinion.

quiz.text: What are the three areas of the Digital House?
options: Search, social, and video
Paid, owned, and earned
Website, advertising, and reporting
Online visibility, content marketing, and targeted digital
quiz.why: The three areas, in order: online visibility, content marketing, targeted digital.

quiz.text: Which prospect is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A business whose site is fast, reviews are strong, and listings are clean
A business that has been burned by digital before — you can explain why it failed
A business with no customers who search online
A business that only wants to buy one tactic
quiz.why: A burned business is cynical — and that cynicism is your best asset, because you can explain why it failed.

quiz.text: A business has a nine-second website, a wrong number in its listings, and six reviews. They want a display campaign. What do you do?
options: Sell the display campaign — it is what they asked for
Decline the business
Show them the deficiencies and propose fixing the foundation first
Sell display at a reduced budget
quiz.why: You cannot advertise your way out of a broken foundation — show the deficiencies and fix the foundation first.

quiz.text: A client with a genuinely strong foundation and good reviews wants advertising. What is the right move?
options: Insist on rebuilding the foundation anyway
Go straight to the roof — the model is a sequence, not a requirement to buy three tiers
Start with content marketing regardless
Run an audit before agreeing to anything
quiz.why: The model is a sequence for deciding where to start — if the foundation is solid, go straight to the roof.

quiz.text: What makes this approach hard for a competitor to copy?
options: The tactics are exclusive to us
Competitors are not allowed to sell in this order
It is a diagnostic method and an order of operations, not a rate on a tactic
It requires a proprietary advertising platform
quiz.why: Everyone else walks in with a rate on a tactic — this is a diagnosis and a sequence, which a price cannot match.

quiz.text: When someone searches “coffee shop near me,” how does Google mostly decide which businesses show at the top?
options: Whoever has the biggest website
Whoever spends the most on radio ads
Whoever is nearby and has a complete, active profile
It’s random each time
quiz.why: Google favors businesses that are close by and have a complete, active profile — that’s the local pack.

quiz.text: A customer finds a restaurant’s profile and taps “Directions” without opening the website. This shows that…
options: The profile itself can turn a search straight into a visit
The website must be broken
The customer made a mistake
Directions don’t really matter
quiz.why: The listing does the selling — action buttons like Directions and Call close the customer right on the profile.

quiz.text: Two plumbers show up. One has recent reviews and replies to them; the other has none. Who’s more likely to get the call — and why?
options: The one with no reviews, because it looks newer
Neither — reviews don’t affect calls
Whichever is first alphabetically
The one with reviews and replies, because it looks active and trustworthy
quiz.why: Reviews and owner replies are trust signals — they tell customers and Google this is a real, cared-for business.

quiz.text: What is the “local pack”?
options: A subscription you buy from Google
The small map with the top few local businesses at the top of a nearby search
A folder of business documents
A type of paid ad
quiz.why: The local pack is that map with the top few local businesses at the top of a “near me” search.

quiz.text: You Google a business by name and a box appears with its hours, phone, photos, and reviews. That box is the…
options: Landing page
Local pack
Knowledge panel
Homepage
quiz.why: That’s the knowledge panel — the info box that appears when you search a business by name.

quiz.text: “Verifying” a Google Business Profile means…
options: Paying a monthly fee
Automatically getting five-star reviews
Linking a social media account
Proving to Google you’re the real owner so you can manage it
quiz.why: Verification is Google confirming you’re the real owner — usually with a code — so you can manage the listing.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit for a Google Business Profile, and why?
options: A national online-only retailer, because it ships everywhere
A local diner, because people choose where to eat from the photos, hours, and reviews
A business with no customers
A company that only sells to the government
quiz.why: GBP shines when a customer is nearby, ready to act, and deciding on their phone — like picking a diner.

quiz.text: A small-town hardware store has the wrong hours and no photos on Google. A shopper searching nearby will most likely…
options: Pick the competitor whose profile looks complete and correct
Call to double-check the hours
Drive over anyway
Wait until tomorrow
quiz.why: The profile is the first impression — a bare or wrong listing loses the customer to a complete one.

quiz.text: Which of these can a business owner actually do with their Google Business Profile?
options: Delete a competitor’s listing
Change Google’s results for everyone
Reply to customer reviews
See customers’ private phone numbers
quiz.why: Owners can reply to reviews, post updates, add photos, and fix info — not control competitors or Google itself.

quiz.text: In the diner example, what actually changed after the profile was claimed and updated?
options: The food got better
They stopped taking walk-ins
They deleted all their reviews
The profile finally matched the quality of the real place, and more people came in saying they found it on Google
quiz.why: Nothing magic — the profile just finally looked as good as the actual diner, so more people found and trusted it.

quiz.text: What does “built for one job” mean for this platform?
options: It only supports single-page websites
It was designed from the start to turn visitors into contacts, rather than adapted from a general-purpose builder
It can only be used by one industry
It handles one client at a time
quiz.why: Designed from the beginning to turn visitors into contacts — not a general-purpose builder with a template on top.

quiz.text: Which of these is included rather than sold separately?
options: Broadcast production
Geofencing
Search and answer engine optimization, the AI chatbot, accessibility, and targeted landing pages
Programmatic audio
quiz.why: Those four are all included in Fourge — one line instead of four separate conversations.

quiz.text: How does a client request a change to their site?
options: They log into a dashboard and make it themselves
They submit a ticket and wait in a queue
They hire a developer
They tell us, and we make it
quiz.why: Fully managed — no dashboard; the client tells us and we make the change.

quiz.text: A “proprietary platform” means…
options: A platform that requires a licence fee
A platform a company built and owns rather than licensed from somebody else
A platform that only works on certain devices
A platform with restricted features
quiz.why: Built and owned by us — which is why nobody else in the market can offer it.

quiz.text: What is AEO?
options: Automated email optimization
Advanced e-commerce operations
Answer engine optimization — being cited by AI assistants when somebody asks a question
Annual expenditure on advertising
quiz.why: AEO is about getting cited by AI assistants when somebody asks a question.

quiz.text: A “brochure site” is…
options: A site built for printing
A site with an online catalogue
A site under five pages
A site that exists, looks respectable, and gives a visitor no obvious next step
quiz.why: It exists and looks fine but does nothing — no obvious next step. That’s what you’re replacing.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A business with a fast, well-maintained current site
An owner who enjoys building and controlling their own website
A carpet cleaning company, because its customers are on a phone needing help today
A business with no customers who search online
quiz.why: When customers need help today on a phone, speed is the whole thing.

quiz.text: An owner says their website is fine — they looked at it this morning. What’s the honest answer?
options: They are probably right
They looked on a laptop on office wifi; their customer is on a phone on mobile data
Site speed only matters for e-commerce
The site is fine but the content needs work
quiz.why: The owner’s test conditions aren’t the customer’s — laptop and office wifi hide the problem.

quiz.text: What is the single best qualifying question for this product?
options: “What’s your advertising budget?”
“Who built your website?”
“When was the last time anything changed on your website?”
“How many pages do you have?”
quiz.why: A shrug is a qualified prospect — nothing sorts them faster.

quiz.text: In the carpet cleaning example, why did they win the job?
options: They were cheaper than the competition
They had better reviews
Their site opened, and the competitors’ did not
They ran a promotion that month
quiz.why: They won it by opening — the first site that actually loaded.

quiz.text: A client runs search ads, has a good listing, and is on the radio — but their website is slow and confusing. What’s the honest first recommendation?
options: Sell them more advertising to make up the difference
Tell them digital doesn’t work for their industry
Fix the website first, because every other dollar they spend lands there
Nothing — the website has no effect on advertising results
quiz.why: Everything else you sell sends a person to the website — a bucket with holes wastes every dollar poured in.

quiz.text: What’s the difference between a website that exists and a website that works?
options: One is a business card; one loads fast, works on a phone, and makes the next step obvious
There isn’t one — being online is enough
A working website simply has more pages
A working website costs more to build
quiz.why: Existing is a business card; working is a salesperson — fast, thumb-friendly, one obvious action.

quiz.text: Why is a monthly arrangement a better fit for a small business than a one-time website build?
options: It isn’t — a one-time build is always the better deal
Because monthly is easier for the salesperson to sell
Because it’s not legal to buy a website outright
The site needs constant upkeep, and the things that make it work — support, security, accessibility, chatbot, analytics — come included instead of bought one at a time
quiz.why: Nine separate products, bills, and renewal dates fold into one predictable amount — and it stays watched in month twenty-four.

quiz.text: What’s the difference between a domain and hosting?
options: They’re two words for the same thing
The domain is the address people type; hosting is the space the site actually lives on
The domain is the design; hosting is the writing
Hosting is the address; the domain is the security
quiz.why: Domain is the address; hosting is the lot the building sits on — different things.

quiz.text: The little padlock in a browser’s address bar indicates…
options: That the site is finished
That the business paid for advertising
SSL — the information going back and forth is scrambled so it can’t be read in transit
That the site is registered with the government
quiz.why: The padlock is SSL — it scrambles information in transit, and browsers warn people off sites without it.

quiz.text: A “landing page” is best described as…
options: The first page of any website
A page that only works on phones
A page that lists every service a business offers
One page built for one offer with one action, with the distractions stripped out
quiz.why: A landing page does one thing — one offer, one action, no menu full of distractions.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A business with no customers and no advertising
A contractor already paying for advertising, because the site is where all of that traffic lands
A business that only sells to one existing client
A national brand with an in-house web team
quiz.why: Anybody already paying for attention needs a place for it to land — the bucket-with-holes conversation.

quiz.text: An owner says, “We don’t need a website — just look us up on Facebook.” What’s the strongest response?
options: Agree, and sell them something else instead
Tell them their Facebook page is worthless
Explain that social media is going away soon

Agree that everyone’s on social, then do the math — the platform shows a post to only a couple percent of their own followers, so they need both: social to be noticed, the site to be checked out and bought from
quiz.why: It’s both, not either — social gets them noticed on rented land; the website is the part they own.

quiz.text: Most people who visit a website never fill anything out. What does visitor identification do about that?
options: Nothing — anonymous visitors can’t be reached
Blocks anonymous visitors from the site
Turns some of those anonymous visitors into known contacts worth following up with
Shows visitors’ private passwords
quiz.why: It turns some anonymous visitors into a name — a real contact where before there was a ghost.

quiz.text: In the flooring-company example, what actually changed?
options: They started installing better floors
The site got fast and easy on a phone, made calling obvious, answered questions after hours — and stopped getting in the way
They lowered their prices
They stopped advertising entirely
quiz.why: Nothing about the company changed — the website just finally stopped getting in the way.

quiz.text: What does the chatbot actually know?
options: Everything about the industry in general
Only what it’s been taught about that specific business
Whatever it finds on competitors’ websites
Only the information on the homepage
quiz.why: It knows what it’s been told about that specific business — services, hours, policies — and nothing more.

quiz.text: What’s the second half of the chatbot’s job, after answering the question?
options: Closing the sale
Directing the visitor to a phone number
Capturing the visitor’s name and contact details so somebody can follow up
Recording the conversation for training
quiz.why: The second half is where the money is — a name and a way to reach them turns a visitor into a warm lead.

quiz.text: Why should limits be set on what the chatbot can commit to?
options: To reduce the number of conversations it handles
Because a business can be held to what its own website says
Because AI cannot process numbers
To keep conversations shorter
quiz.why: Quoting prices or promising outcomes is an owner’s deliberate decision, not something a bot improvises.

quiz.text: “Training” in this context means…
options: Teaching staff how to use the chat window
Loading the business’s own information in — services, hours, policies, common questions
The chatbot learning from competitors over time
A practice period before the bot goes live
quiz.why: Training is the setup step — what it’s taught is what it knows, and nothing more.

quiz.text: “Escalation” means…
options: Increasing the number of questions the bot will answer
Raising the chatbot’s position on the page
Handing a conversation off to a human when it goes past what the bot should handle
Following up with a visitor a second time
quiz.why: Every good setup has one — and a client should always ask where those conversations go.

quiz.text: “Lead capture” refers to…
options: Counting how many people opened the chat
Collecting a visitor’s name and contact details during the conversation
Recording which pages a visitor viewed
Blocking spam messages
quiz.why: Lead capture is the part that turns a chat into business — a contact somebody can follow up with.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A business that answers its phone all day and gets very little website traffic
A business unwilling to keep its information current
A martial arts school, because parents research at night when nobody’s there to answer
A company with no website
quiz.why: The strongest fits get the same questions constantly, at hours when nobody’s there to answer them.

quiz.text: A client wants a chat window but has nobody to monitor it. What’s the argument for an AI chatbot specifically?
options: A live chat window is always the better option
A small business can’t staff chat at nine-thirty at night, and an unattended window is worse than none at all
AI chat costs more but looks more professional
Chat windows don’t need monitoring
quiz.why: An unattended chat window disappoints people — the honest case for AI is having something reliable there.

quiz.text: What happens if the business changes its hours and nobody updates the chatbot?
options: It stops answering questions about hours
It automatically detects the change
It keeps confidently telling people the old hours
It escalates every question to a human
quiz.why: It only knows what it’s taught — somebody has to keep it current, or it confidently gives the old hours.

quiz.text: In the martial arts example, what actually changed?
options: They extended their class schedule
They hired somebody to answer the phone at night
They lowered their monthly tuition
A nighttime question got answered in seconds and a contact was captured, so the owner called a parent who’d already decided
quiz.why: Not a sales pitch — one answer, at the moment somebody needed it, and a captured contact to call back.

quiz.text: A restaurant’s entire menu is one photograph. What does a customer using a screen reader experience?
options: The screen reader reads the menu items aloud
The screen reader describes the food automatically
The site converts the photo to text for them
They hear the word “image” and get nothing else
quiz.why: A screen reader reads whatever written description exists — with none, it just says “image,” and that’s the customer’s whole experience.

quiz.text: What’s the point of the accessibility panel being adjustable by the visitor?
options: It lets the business guess what most people need
The person adjusts the site to their own needs in seconds, rather than the business guessing
It removes the need for the site to work properly underneath
It only changes how the site looks to the business owner
quiz.why: The visitor chooses — they adjust the site to themselves in about four seconds, instead of the business guessing.

quiz.text: Why is accessibility something that has to be maintained rather than finished?
options: Because the guidelines are rewritten every month
Because the tool expires and needs replacing
Because a site changes constantly — new pages, unlabeled photos, redesigned sections — and each change can break what was working
It doesn’t; once a site is fixed it stays fixed
quiz.why: Accessibility is a condition you maintain, like security — any change can break what was fine last month.

quiz.text: What is “alt text”?
options: The written description attached to an image so a screen reader can say what it is
A backup version of a web page
Text that appears when a page fails to load
An alternate language version of the site
quiz.why: Alt text is the written description attached to an image — the smallest, most skipped, highest-impact item on the list.

quiz.text: “WCAG” is best described as…
options: A federal agency that inspects websites
A piece of software installed on a site
The guidelines that serve as the yardstick for accessibility, with double-A as the common target
A certification a business buys once
quiz.why: WCAG is the rulebook — the yardstick — and double-A is the level most businesses and courts treat as the target.

quiz.text: The ADA is…
options: A web design standard written for the internet
A voluntary industry best practice
A rule that applies only to government agencies
A civil rights law that courts have applied to websites
quiz.why: The ADA is a civil rights law — older than the modern internet — and courts have applied it to websites.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A wholesaler with three longtime customers and no public site
A hearing clinic, because nearly every patient it serves is in the group that benefits most
A business with no website at all
A business whose customers are all under thirty
quiz.why: Businesses whose customers are mostly older are barely a pitch — you’re describing the people in their waiting room.

quiz.text: An owner asks you point-blank whether this will keep them from getting sued. What do you say?
options: That it reduces risk and shows a good-faith effort, but legal questions are for their attorney
Yes — that’s the main thing it does
That lawsuits over websites aren’t a real concern
That you’ll put the guarantee in writing
quiz.why: You are not an attorney — never promise lawsuit-proof. It reduces risk and shows good faith; specifics go to their attorney.

quiz.text: Besides helping people with disabilities, what else does accessibility work tend to do?
options: Nothing else — the benefit is limited to that group
It slows the site down as a tradeoff
It requires removing images and video from the site
It makes the site better for everyone — outdoors, one-handed, sound off — and the structure helps search engines too
quiz.why: The curb cut, again — bigger targets, higher contrast, captions help everyone, and the structure a screen reader needs helps search engines.

quiz.text: In the hearing-clinic example, what actually changed?
options: The clinic started treating different patients
The clinic removed its website
Patients could adjust the site themselves and read it without help, and the content became readable by screen readers and keyboards
The clinic stopped taking older patients
quiz.why: Nothing about the clinic changed — the website finally matched the care they already gave.

quiz.text: Which of these is part of the technical cleanup on a website?
options: Writing more social media posts
Buying a higher spot in the search results
Speeding up the site, fixing what’s broken, making it work on a phone, and making sure every page can be found
Raising the client’s prices
quiz.why: The foundation is the technical layer — speed, mobile, broken links, a findable index, and the padlock.

quiz.text: What’s the best way to handle the questions customers ask before they buy?
options: Answer them plainly on the website, in the page headline and a Q&A section
Keep them off the website so people have to call
Put them all on one page in tiny print
Only answer them in a monthly email
quiz.why: The answers mechanic: one page, one question, answered plainly — which is exactly what an AI wants to quote.

quiz.text: Two contractors have equally nice websites. One is linked to and listed by other credible sites; the other only talks about itself. Who’s more likely to be named — and why?
options: The one that only talks about itself, because it controls the message
Neither — links and listings don’t affect anything
Whichever one is older
The one other sites back up, because outside evidence is what search engines and AI trust
quiz.why: Authority is about who else vouches for you — links, listings, and reviews are the evidence an AI digs through.

quiz.text: What are “organic results”?
options: The listings marked “Sponsored”
The unpaid listings a business earns rather than buys
A type of monthly subscription
Results that only show on phones
quiz.why: Organic results are the unpaid listings — anything not marked Sponsored.

quiz.text: A “backlink” is…
options: A link back to your own homepage
A broken link that needs fixing
A link from another website pointing to yours
A paid placement on a search page
quiz.why: A backlink is another site linking to yours — a vote of confidence.

quiz.text: The A.I.-written summary paragraph that appears above the regular search listings is called…
options: A sponsored result
A backlink
A landing page
An AI Overview
quiz.why: That top summary is the AI Overview — the box people mean when they say “AI is eating search.”

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit for SEO and AEO, and why?
options: A roadside stand that only takes cash from passing traffic
A local roofing company, because people research a big repair for days and type real questions the whole time
A business with no website and no plans for one
A company that only sells to one existing customer
quiz.why: SEO/AEO shines when the customer researches before buying — a big repair means days of searching.

quiz.text: A homeowner asks their phone whether a cracked tooth needs a crown. The A.I. answers and names two local dentists — your client isn’t one. What most likely happened?
options: The patient got helped, picked from the two that were named, and never visited your client’s site
The A.I. is broken
The patient will search again tomorrow
Nothing — the A.I. answer doesn’t affect who gets called
quiz.why: People get answered and decide without clicking — if you’re not named, you never got invited.

quiz.text: Which of these is part of the work on an SEO and AEO campaign?
options: Buying guaranteed placement at the top of Google
Deleting competitors’ websites
Cleaning up technical issues, optimizing pages, creating content that answers real questions, and building outside credibility
Writing the A.I.’s answers directly
quiz.why: The campaign is cleanup + on-page + content + credibility — you can’t buy your way into organic or the AI answer.

quiz.text: In the roofing example, what actually changed?
options: They lowered their prices
They went from one page that said nothing to pages that plainly answered what homeowners were already asking
They stopped answering the phone
They removed their website
quiz.why: They stopped shouting and started answering — a page for each service and a plain-English FAQ.

quiz.text: An HVAC company offers three services and works in four towns. Using the grid idea, how many pages does that suggest?
options: One page listing all three services
Twelve — one for each service in each town
Four — one per town, listing everything
Three — one per service, no towns named
quiz.why: The grid: services down one side, towns across the top — a page for every square. Three services × four towns = twelve.

quiz.text: Why does a targeted landing page need the town named in the headline and the writing?
options: So the business can charge more for the page
It doesn’t matter where the town is mentioned
Because towns must legally be listed on a website
So the page matches what the person actually typed and reads as the closest answer
quiz.why: Match the search — naming the service and town makes the page the closest answer to what someone typed.

quiz.text: What makes these “landing” pages rather than just extra pages?
options: Each one is built to get one clear action — call, book, or directions
They only work on mobile phones
They replace the homepage
They can only be reached from an ad
quiz.why: A landing page exists to get one thing to happen — that’s the “one clear action” mechanic.

quiz.text: “Search intent” means…
options: The number of times a keyword appears on a page
How much a business is willing to spend
What the person searching actually wants — browsing versus ready to call
The order results appear in
quiz.why: Search intent is what the person actually wants — a broad word means looking around; a service plus a town means ready to call.

quiz.text: In “roof repair in Franklin,” which part is the location keyword?
options: “Roof repair”
“In Franklin”
Both halves equally
Neither — that’s a service keyword only
quiz.why: The location keyword is the place half — “in Franklin.” “Roof repair” is the service half.

quiz.text: A business’s “service area” is…
options: The section of the website listing its services
The room where the work gets done
The single town where its office is located
All the towns it actually serves, which is usually more than where its office sits
quiz.why: Service area is every town a business serves — the gap between that and the office town is the whole opportunity.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A plumbing company whose office is in one town but who drives to six
An online-only retailer that ships nationwide
A business with one service and one location and no plans to grow
A company with no website
quiz.why: The gap between where the office sits and where they’ll drive is exactly what these pages capture.

quiz.text: A roofer works in five towns but his site never names any of them. What’s most likely happening?
options: Search engines assume he covers the whole state
Nothing — town names don’t affect search
People in four of those towns don’t find him, because nothing says he’ll come out there
His homepage automatically ranks in all five
quiz.why: They’re invisible in most of the area they serve — nothing on the site says he’ll come out there.

quiz.text: Why is it a problem to build these pages by copying one page and swapping the town name?
options: It isn’t — that’s the fastest way to do it
Search engines can spot copied, thin pages, and those can do more harm than good
Copying is fine as long as the headline changes
Because each page has to be a different color
quiz.why: Thin, cookie-cutter pages can do more harm than good — each page has to really be about that service in that town.

quiz.text: In the insurance-agency example, what actually changed?
options: They started selling different kinds of insurance
They opened offices in five new towns
They lowered their premiums
They already served those towns — the website finally said so, with a page for each service in each town
quiz.why: Nothing about the business changed — the website finally said what they’d been doing all along, one page per service per town.

quiz.text: What’s the difference between a business’s own list and an acquired list?
options: There’s no real difference in how people respond
Acquired lists are illegal to use
Their own list is customers who already know them; an acquired list reaches new people, and strangers respond differently
Their own list can’t be emailed without permission from the platform
quiz.why: Their own list half-expects to hear from them; strangers on an acquired list respond differently.

quiz.text: Who should the email be written to?
options: The business owner, since they’re approving it
Nobody in particular — keep it general so it fits everyone
The industry, like a blog post about the category
The advertiser’s customer, in the advertiser’s voice — fewer “we” and “our,” more “you” and “your”
quiz.why: Written to their customer, in their voice — that distinction is the whole program.

quiz.text: Why does consistency matter more than any single email?
options: Because the law requires a minimum number of sends
Because the first email never gets delivered
It doesn’t — one good email is enough
Showing up regularly makes the business recognizable, and reporting after each send shows what landed
quiz.why: One email isn’t a campaign — the rhythm is what makes a business recognizable.

quiz.text: “Preview text” is…
options: A draft version of the email before it’s sent
The short line of copy the inbox shows after the subject line
The first image in the email
A test send to the client
quiz.why: It’s the gray line after the subject — a second chance to get somebody in.

quiz.text: A business has a strong open rate but almost nobody clicks. Where’s the problem most likely?
options: The subject line
The send day
The offer or the button inside the email
The unsubscribe link
quiz.why: Strong opens, weak clicks points at the offer or the button, not the subject line.

quiz.text: Why is the unsubscribe link a good thing, not just a legal requirement?
options: Because people who can’t escape mark it as spam, which hurts future delivery for everyone
Because it makes the list grow faster
Because it’s required to include images
It isn’t — it should be hidden as well as possible
quiz.why: A trapped reader marks spam instead of leaving, which hurts everyone’s deliverability.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A business selling one thing once to strangers who’ll never return
A company with no customer contact information at all
A business that only sells through a single wholesale buyer
A salon, because people buy repeatedly and the whole game is being remembered at the right moment
quiz.why: Repeat-purchase businesses win on being remembered — the inbox is the cheapest reminder.

quiz.text: An owner mentions he has a few hundred customer addresses in a spreadsheet he’s never used. What’s the opportunity?
options: Nothing — old addresses are worthless
He already owns an audience aimed at his cheapest-to-sell customers, and it’s doing nothing
He should sell the list to another business
He needs to start over and collect new addresses
quiz.why: It’s money on the floor — an owned audience of the cheapest customers to sell, unused.

quiz.text: A client asks what the best day to send is. What’s the best answer?
options: There’s one correct day that works for every business
Whenever the client happens to have time
Generally Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday — though it’s industry-dependent
Weekends, because inboxes are emptier
quiz.why: Mid-week mornings generally, but it depends on the business — an honest, informed answer.

quiz.text: In the storage-company example, what actually changed?
options: He started emailing past renters he’d never contacted — short, mobile-friendly, written for the renter rather than about the company
He built new storage buildings
He lowered his monthly rates
He bought a list of strangers
quiz.why: He started talking to people who’d already trusted him once — written for the renter.

quiz.text: A client sells commercial equipment to other businesses. Which channel is the most natural fit?
options: TikTok, because the videos are short
Snapchat, because it’s private
LinkedIn, because it’s the professional, business-to-business room
Pinterest, because people plan purchases there
quiz.why: LinkedIn is the office — the B2B room and the highest-income crowd.

quiz.text: Why does a strategist write thoughtful content instead of making every post promotional?
options: Because promotional posts are against platform rules
Because thoughtful posts are faster to write
Nobody follows a business to be sold to repeatedly — useful content earns attention, so the occasional ask actually lands
Because promotional content can’t be boosted
quiz.why: Content that earns attention before it asks for anything is what makes the ask land.

quiz.text: Eight posts go out in a month and two get boosted. Why pick those two after publishing rather than in advance?
options: Because boosting only works on older posts
Because the platform requires a waiting period
It doesn’t matter — the timing is arbitrary
Because you can see which posts people actually responded to, then put money behind the proven ones
quiz.why: Post first, watch what works, then spend on the proven one — not a guess.

quiz.text: “Reach” means…
options: How many followers an account has
How many actual people saw the post
How far away the customers live
How many platforms a business is on
quiz.why: Reach is how many real people saw it — a thousand followers doesn’t mean a thousand see everything.

quiz.text: What is an “organic post”?
options: A post about health or natural products
A post that has been boosted
A post that only followers can see
Anything a business posts without paying to promote it
quiz.why: Organic just means unpaid — and it reaches only a fraction of the followers.

quiz.text: The “algorithm” is best described as…
options: The platform’s system for deciding who sees what, based partly on early engagement
A tool businesses buy to schedule posts
The total number of likes a post receives
A rule requiring businesses to post daily
quiz.why: It watches early engagement and shows the post more widely if people react.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A concrete supplier selling to three longtime contractors
A business with no customers yet
A garden center, because it’s visual and always has something seasonal to announce
A company that only bids on government contracts
quiz.why: Something to show and something to say on a regular basis — the calendar writes itself.

quiz.text: An owner says social media doesn’t work — she posted three times and barely anyone saw it. What’s actually going on?
options: Her followers have all left the platform
Platforms show free posts to only a fraction of followers, so good posts can go unseen without paid help
She posted at the wrong time of day, and that’s the whole issue
Nothing — if a post doesn’t perform, the business isn’t a fit
quiz.why: Posting isn’t the same as being seen — which is exactly why the paid piece matters.

quiz.text: Why are social media management and social media advertising described as a one-two punch?
options: Because they’re sold by two different departments
Because advertising replaces the need to post
Because management is cheaper than advertising
Management keeps the business present and credible; advertising reaches people who’ve never heard of them
quiz.why: Management is the jab, advertising the right hand — each makes the other work.

quiz.text: In the garden-center example, what actually changed?
options: They started posting regularly and answering comments, and put money behind the post that took off
They began growing different plants
They opened a second location
They deleted their old account and started over
quiz.why: Regular posts, same-day replies, and a boost on the one that earned it.

quiz.text: What does the client need to provide?
options: A script and some images
Raw audio that our team then edits and mixes
Access to their existing video and photography library
A finished, produced radio spot
quiz.why: A finished, produced spot.

quiz.text: Who builds the visuals?
options: The client’s own marketing team
An automated tool that matches images to the audio
Our video team
The platform
quiz.why: Our video team builds them.

quiz.text: What comes back?
options: A finished video, ready to run
A storyboard to approve
A set of image files for the client to assemble
An edited audio file with suggested visual timings
quiz.why: Finished and ready to run.

quiz.text: “Radio to video” describes…
options: Producing a new commercial from an existing script
Turning a finished radio spot into a video ad
Simulcasting radio online
Adapting a television commercial for radio broadcast
quiz.why: Finished radio spot in, video ad out.

quiz.text: A “fully produced spot” means the audio is…
options: Longer than thirty seconds
Recorded but not yet mixed or mastered
Cleared for use across all advertising media
Finished — voiced, mixed, and ready to air
quiz.why: Voiced, mixed, ready to air.

quiz.text: “Social-style video” refers to…
options: Video posted directly to social platforms
Clean visuals built to work with sound off
Content produced by a social media manager
A vertical format designed for mobile viewing
quiz.why: Built to work with sound off.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A client who is expecting a professionally filmed television commercial
A business with no radio schedule and no audio creative
An auto repair shop already running radio, with no video
A client who wants the spot’s wording changed for video
quiz.why: Already running radio, no video.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: It unlocks the video products a client was blocked from buying
A lower production cost than filming a commercial
A finished commercial that is fully suitable for broadcast television
Ongoing video content produced each month
quiz.why: It unlocks the video products.

quiz.text: A client says their radio spot isn’t a video. What do you say?
options: Agree with them, and suggest they commission a proper video production instead
Explain that most video ads are made this way
Offer to send an example and let them decide
They’ve already paid for the hard half — the audio is done
quiz.why: The hard half is done.

quiz.text: What must be set at the first meeting?
options: Which platforms the video will run on
How many versions will be produced
What it is and what it isn’t
That visuals get approved
quiz.why: Expectation — not a film crew.

quiz.text: Why is the audit such an effective sales tool?
options: It predicts how much revenue the client will gain
It shows the owner his own incorrect information on a screen, so you don’t have to convince him of anything
It guarantees top rankings
It removes the need for any ongoing work
quiz.why: It’s his own information, wrong, on screen — nothing to argue about.

quiz.text: An owner says he already fixed his address on Google. Why isn’t that enough?
options: Google doesn’t accept address changes
He needs to fix it on his website instead
His information also lives on seventy-plus other directories, apps, and databases that never got the update
It is enough — Google feeds every other site automatically
quiz.why: Google is one of seventy-plus places the data lives — the rest still have the old info.

quiz.text: A client cancels after six months because his listings are all correct now. What’s the best response?
options: Agree that the work is complete
Offer to re-clean the listings at a discount
Explain that directories rarely change anything
It’s the oil in the car — data drifts back to the old information, so accuracy is maintained, not purchased once
quiz.why: The engine running smooth is the oil doing its job — stop and it drifts back.

quiz.text: “NAP” stands for…
options: Name, address, phone number
New account profile
Network access point
Name and physical address
quiz.why: Name, address, phone — the three pieces that must match everywhere.

quiz.text: A “data aggregator” is…
options: A tool that counts how many listings a business has
A company that collects business data in bulk and feeds it to many directories at once
A type of duplicate listing
Software that writes business descriptions
quiz.why: The wholesalers — which is how one bad record spreads to a dozen sites.

quiz.text: What problem does a duplicate listing cause?
options: It doubles the business’s visibility
None — extra listings are always helpful
It splits reviews and signals, and makes search engines unsure which record is real
It only affects paid advertising
quiz.why: Two records split the reviews and confuse the search engine.

quiz.text: Which business is an especially strong fit, and why?
options: A business that has never changed its name, address, phone, or hours
An online-only seller with no physical location or phone
A one-person consultancy with no public address
A clinic that moved across town, because its old address is still live on dozens of directories
quiz.why: Any change scatters across dozens of places that never got the memo.

quiz.text: A customer calls the number she found in a map app and it rings nowhere. What does she most likely do next?
options: Search for a different number for that business
Call the competitor instead — and she may not use that business again
Drive to the location to check
Wait and try again tomorrow
quiz.why: Wrong information doesn’t confuse people, it loses them — to the competitor.

quiz.text: Why does fixing listings make a client’s other digital spending work better?
options: It doesn’t — the two are unrelated
Because it lowers advertising costs directly
Because directories give discounts to managed listings
Search engines trust a business more when its information matches everywhere, so it ranks better
quiz.why: Matching data is trust; mismatched data is doubt — and trust ranks higher.

quiz.text: In the clinic example, what actually changed?
options: The clinic moved back to its old location
The clinic hired more staff
One correct record everywhere, the duplicate cleared, and somebody watching so a later re-import got caught
The clinic stopped accepting new patients
quiz.why: One source of truth, duplicate cleared, and monitoring caught the re-import.

quiz.text: A shop with 10 reviews at 4.5 gets one 1-star, dropping to ~4.2. A shop with 100 reviews at 4.5 gets the same 1-star. What happens?
options: It drops just as much, since one review is one review
It barely moves — around 4.47 — which is why volume is the strategy
The review is automatically removed
Its rating goes up
quiz.why: Volume is the armor — with 100 reviews one bad night barely registers.

quiz.text: Why does the program collect the client’s customer list every month rather than once at signup?
options: Because review links expire after 30 days
Because Google requires a monthly upload
To replace the need for QR codes
There’s a fresh batch of customers every month, and volume only builds if the asking never stops
quiz.why: Reviews expire and new customers arrive monthly — the asking can’t stop.

quiz.text: What does the feedback step actually change for a business owner?
options: It prevents unhappy customers from posting reviews
It removes negative reviews already published
It changes who finds out first — the owner the same day, instead of reading it on Google weeks later
It replaces the need to respond to reviews
quiz.why: Same feature, stated accurately: who finds out first, not suppression.

quiz.text: “Review velocity” refers to…
options: How fast the business replies to reviews
How recently and steadily new reviews are arriving
How quickly a review is posted after a purchase
The total number of reviews
quiz.why: Velocity is recency and steadiness — a stalled profile looks like it used to be good.

quiz.text: Why does a business with 6 five-star reviews often look worse than one with 200 at 4.6?
options: Because five stars is a bad score
Because older reviews count more
