Because six reviews looks unproven — volume reads as evidence
Because Google hides businesses with few reviews
quiz.why: 47% won’t use a business under twenty reviews — the count alone disqualifies.

quiz.text: Besides Google, where else should a business’s reviews be monitored?
options: Nowhere — Google is the only one that counts
Only on the business’s own website
Only on Facebook
Facebook, Yelp, and whichever site matters most in that specific industry
quiz.why: Watch everywhere — including the industry site the owner never logs into.

quiz.text: You look up a prospect and see 4.1 stars with 22 reviews. What does that tell you?
options: They’re above the national average and don’t need help
The score is fine; only the review count matters
They’re below the national average of about 4.4 and thin on volume — a strong prospect on both counts
Nothing useful without seeing the individual reviews
quiz.why: Below 4.4 and low volume — qualified on both the score and the count.

quiz.text: Two shops are equally close and relevant to a search. One has more reviews, a better score, and recent activity. What happens?
options: Google shows them in alphabetical order
The one with the better review profile gets shown first
Reviews have no effect on which businesses appear
Google shows whichever spends more on ads
quiz.why: Review signals help decide who gets shown at all — not just who persuades.

quiz.text: Why is replying to a negative review worth doing?
options: It gets the review deleted
It hides the review from search results
The next customer reads the response, and a calm reply makes the business look like it cares
It’s required by Google
quiz.why: The next customer reads the response, not just the complaint.

quiz.text: In the auto-shop example, what actually changed?
options: They hired all new mechanics
They got the old negative review removed
They lowered their labor rate
They started asking everyone, added QR cards, replied to reviews, and let volume raise the score
quiz.why: Ask everybody, reply, and let volume do the work — the scoreboard matched the shop.

quiz.text: What does “buy the moment” mean?
options: Buying the cheapest clicks
Reserving a fixed position at the top of the results page each day
The ad appears when somebody searches for what the client sells
Bidding only during the hours the business is open to take calls
quiz.why: The ad shows up at the moment of the search.

quiz.text: What does “match the promise” require?
options: The landing page delivers what the ad offered
Reusing the website headline
Every keyword appears somewhere in the ad text
The offer stays unchanged for the full campaign flight
quiz.why: The page must deliver what the ad offered.

quiz.text: “Control the waste” is mostly about…
options: Lowering the daily budget
Reducing the number of keywords each month
Pausing the campaign whenever the phone gets busy
Negative keywords, scheduling, and shifting budget
quiz.why: Negatives, scheduling, and moving budget.

quiz.text: A “negative keyword” does what?
options: Lowers the bid on that term
Stops the ad showing for searches you don't want
Flags a competitor's brand name for exclusion
Marks a keyword as too expensive to continue
quiz.why: It blocks searches that never convert.

quiz.text: “Pay-per-click” means the advertiser owes money…
options: Each time the ad is displayed on a results page
When a click leads to a phone call or a form
Only when somebody clicks
Monthly, as a flat fee
quiz.why: Being shown costs nothing; a click costs.

quiz.text: “Quality Score” is roughly a measure of…
options: How relevant the keyword, ad, and landing page are to each other
The creative standard of the ad's design
How much competitors are bidding on the same terms
The client's account history and payment record
quiz.why: It grades relevance across keyword, ad, and page.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business whose customers never search online for what it sells
A brand-new business with no website to send traffic to
A client who wants the cheapest cost per thousand impressions
A plumber, because people search at the moment something breaks
quiz.why: Urgent need — whoever's at the top gets the call.

quiz.text: What does the advertiser get that no other tactic offers?
options: The lowest cost per thousand available
An audience that asked to be shown options
Guaranteed placement above all competitors
Reporting within twenty-four hours of the start
quiz.why: An audience that asked to be shown options.

quiz.text: A client says search ads didn't work when they tried them. What do you ask?
options: Whether they used the correct billing currency and time zone
How much they spent each month versus competitors
Whether the ad pointed at the homepage, and whether there were negatives
Suggest they try a different platform this time
quiz.why: Both failures are management, not the tactic.

quiz.text: What should you settle at the first meeting?
options: That clicks are the cost, and calls and forms are the result
That the client won't pause during slower months
That the landing page gets rebuilt first
That results aren't reviewed until three months have run
quiz.why: Frame clicks as the cost, not the result.

quiz.text: What are the two ways to decide who sees the ad?
options: Picking specific websites by hand
Audience targeting and contextual targeting
Selecting a daypart and rotating through available inventory each week
Setting a geographic radius and letting the platform allocate impressions
quiz.why: Audience targeting follows the person; contextual reads the page.

quiz.text: “Programmatic” describes…
options: A software tool the client logs into to manage their own campaign
A schedule of ad placements negotiated directly with each website owner
A reporting dashboard
Automated buying and placing of ads
quiz.why: It is the automated buying method, not a targeting type.

quiz.text: What is the advertiser actually buying?
options: Impressions, with frequency managed
Guaranteed clicks to their website
A fixed number of new customers each month
Placement on a specific list of approved local websites
quiz.why: Impressions, bought by the thousand, with frequency managed.

quiz.text: One “impression” is…
options: One person seeing the ad and remembering the business afterwards
One click on the advertisement
One ad served onto one screen
One thousand opportunities for the advertisement to be seen
quiz.why: One ad served onto one screen — what display is sold on.

quiz.text: “Retargeting” reaches…
options: Nearby households
People who have already visited the client’s site
Customers from a list the client provides from their own records
Anybody who has searched for the client’s category in the last month
quiz.why: People who already visited — the piece clients grasp fastest.

quiz.text: “Contextual targeting” places the ad based on…
options: What the person has previously browsed
The time of day the person is most likely to be online
The demographics of the site’s audience
The content of the page
quiz.why: The content of the page — the ad waits in the right room.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business with no website for traffic to return to
A client who will only judge the campaign on the click column
A garden center, because its customers browse for weeks before buying
A business that needs countable phone calls within the first seven days
quiz.why: A long, browsing decision keeps the business in the conversation the whole time.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit for the advertiser?
options: Reaching people before they start looking
The lowest cost of any tactic in the catalogue
Guaranteed clicks at a fixed rate
A detailed list of every person who saw the advertisement
quiz.why: Display creates demand — it reaches people before they search.

quiz.text: A client says nobody clicks display ads. What is the right response?
options: Explain that click data is unreliable and should be disregarded entirely
Agree — then explain most of what it does never shows up as a click
Point out that their competitors are clicking on the ads regularly
Offer to switch the budget into search advertising instead
quiz.why: Agree first — most responses are view-through and never show as a click.

quiz.text: What must be pre-framed at the first meeting?
options: That the client should not expect any reporting for the first sixty days
That the campaign requires a minimum six-month commitment to work
That display replaces search
That clicks will look low, and that is normal
quiz.why: Pre-frame low clicks in month one so nobody cancels in month three.

quiz.text: How does the advertisement get built?
options: A designer builds each banner by hand
The client uploads finished creative for each audience segment
The platform selects from a library of pre-approved designs
The template fills itself with whatever fits the viewer
quiz.why: The template assembles itself around the viewer.

quiz.text: What decides which version somebody sees?
options: The time of day and the device they happen to be using
What they searched for or read
A preset rotation across all products
The geographic area the person is located in
quiz.why: Search signals and content decide the version.

quiz.text: What keeps the ads accurate?
options: Manual review of every impression
A monthly audit carried out by the client's own staff
Feed accuracy and weekly refinement
Automatic removal of any product not updated within thirty days
quiz.why: Feed accuracy is the thing to watch.

quiz.text: “Dynamic creative” means…
options: An ad that assembles itself per viewer
An animated banner
Creative refreshed by our design team each month
An ad that changes its budget based on daily performance
quiz.why: It assembles itself in the moment.

quiz.text: A “product feed” is…
options: A weekly stock email
The reporting file showing which products ran most
A social stream where the client posts new arrivals
A live list of what the client sells
quiz.why: A live list that fills the template slots.

quiz.text: A “search signal” is…
options: A competitor alert
A notification that somebody clicked the ad
Evidence of what a person has been looking for
The monthly search volume for a product category
quiz.why: Evidence of what a person has been looking for.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business with one product and one price
An RV dealership, because its inventory turns over constantly
A business unwilling to tell us when stock changes
A service business with no inventory to speak of
quiz.why: Constantly-changing inventory is built for this.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Relevance at scale, without building each ad
A cheaper impression rate
Guaranteed clicks from people ready to buy today
A report of which products each viewer looked at
quiz.why: Relevance at scale, without building each ad.

quiz.text: A client asks whether the ads might show something already sold. What do you say?
options: Reassure them the platform prevents this from ever happening
Explain that occasional inaccuracy is normal and not worth worrying about
Recommend they switch to standard display instead
Be straight — that's what feed accuracy is for, and it's the thing to watch
quiz.why: Handle it honestly in the first meeting.

quiz.text: Besides the click pre-frame, what should you agree at the first meeting?
options: Client approval of every version
That the campaign pauses automatically when stock runs low
Who tells us when the inventory changes
That a designer reviews the templates every second week
quiz.why: Agree who tells us when inventory changes.

quiz.text: What does “draw the fence” mean?
options: Defining an area where devices get added to the audience
Setting a radius around the client's own premises
Picking specific websites
Choosing the hours the campaign is permitted to run
quiz.why: Defining the area that builds the audience.

quiz.text: What is “the tail”?
options: The final week of the campaign flight
The delay between entering and the first ad appearing
Continuing to reach the device after it leaves
Budget held back for the end of the month
quiz.why: Reaching the device after it leaves the fence.

quiz.text: How long does that window typically last?
options: Twenty-four hours
Up to about thirty days
Until the device enters a different geofence
The rest of the calendar month of the visit
quiz.why: Up to about thirty days — the decision window.

quiz.text: “Conquesting” means fencing…
options: An event venue during a scheduled occasion
The neighbourhoods where the best customers live
The whole region
A competitor's location
quiz.why: Fencing a competitor's location.

quiz.text: A “point of interest” is…
options: A specific place worth fencing
The client's most-visited web page
A moment when somebody is most likely to act
A recommended budget category
quiz.why: A specific place worth fencing.

quiz.text: “Offline visit attribution” measures…
options: Clicks that became calls
How many devices entered the area in total
Whether devices that saw the ad later visited the client
Which client location got the most foot traffic
quiz.why: Whether ad-exposed devices later visited.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business whose customers never leave home
A client who wants a whole county reached evenly
An online-only retailer with no premises
A hearing clinic, because you can fence the audiologists nearby
quiz.why: You can fence exactly where the audience is.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: The cheapest display option
Buying intent instead of guessing at it
Guaranteed foot traffic in the first month
A list of every device at a competitor
quiz.why: Buying intent instead of guessing at it.

quiz.text: A client asks whether this is creepy. What do you say?
options: Everyone's phone is tracked anyway, so it's normal
Only anonymised names and numbers are used
A device entered an area — no name, no number, and we cap the frequency
Change the subject to how well it works
quiz.why: No name, no number — and we cap frequency.

quiz.text: What is the strongest thing to sell alongside this, where available?
options: Offline visit measurement
A bigger budget
A second search campaign on the same keywords
Extra creative to keep the ad fresh
quiz.why: Offline visit measurement — the closest thing to counting a walk-in.

quiz.text: What is the first step?
options: Booking a booth
Building a list from the organiser's registration data
Picking the event where the right people gather
Setting a radius around the venue for the month
quiz.why: Pick the event where the right people gather.

quiz.text: What happens after the event ends?
options: It stops
The audience merges into the general display campaign
A second fence is drawn around attendees' homes
The tail keeps running for weeks
quiz.why: The tail keeps running through the decision.

quiz.text: “Match the moment” means…
options: Using creative that fits why they were there
Advertising during the event only
Matching campaign length to the event's duration
Aligning budget with expected attendance
quiz.why: Creative that fits why they were there.

quiz.text: The “event window” is…
options: The month after the event when decisions get made
The period the fence is live around the venue
The venue's public opening hours
The booking deadline
quiz.why: The period the fence is live around the venue.

quiz.text: “Post-event retargeting” reaches…
options: People who clicked during the event
Booth visitors only
Anybody living near the venue
Devices that were at the event
quiz.why: Devices that were physically at the event.

quiz.text: “Cross-device matching” lets you…
options: Serve the ad across several formats
Count how many devices one attendee carries
Reach the same household on other screens
Compare device performance
quiz.why: Reach the same household on other screens.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A wedding venue, because expo attendees decide over the following weeks
A business whose customers never attend events
A client who wants results the same day
A business that already sponsors the event
quiz.why: The decision happens in the weeks after the show.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Lower cost than a booth
A pre-qualified audience nobody had to build
Guaranteed leads from every attendee
A record of who visited the stand
quiz.why: A pre-qualified audience nobody had to build.

quiz.text: A client says they already have a booth. What do you say?
options: Suggest they cancel the booth and advertise instead
Explain booths are poor value versus digital
Recommend a different event to avoid overlap
This makes the booth work harder — the ad is still there in week three
quiz.why: The ad keeps working after everyone's gone home.

quiz.text: How do you stop an event client quietly drifting away?
options: Run ninety-day campaigns
Sell from the annual calendar, not one event
Require a twelve-month commitment first
Schedule a review right after each event
quiz.why: Book the year's shows and it's a programme.

quiz.text: What is the first step?
options: Buying a list
Installing a tracking pixel on every page
Segmenting customers by how much they spent
The client's own list becomes a targetable audience
quiz.why: Their own list becomes the audience.

quiz.text: “Speak to them like you know them” means…
options: Creative that reflects that they've already bought
Using their first name
Matching the tone of the client's newsletters
Naming the exact product each customer bought
quiz.why: Creative that reflects they've already bought.

quiz.text: Where does the audience get reached?
options: In their inbox
Only on mobile devices
On websites, apps, and other screens
Only on social platforms they use
quiz.why: Everywhere else — websites, apps, screens.

quiz.text: “First-party data” is…
options: Purchased data
Data the client collected themselves
Behavioural data from website visitors
Segments built by the ad platform
quiz.why: Data the client collected themselves.

quiz.text: “Match rate” is…
options: How much of the list can be reached
The response rate
The share of the list that bought twice
How closely the audience resembles best customers
quiz.why: How much of the list can actually be reached.

quiz.text: “Audience match” describes…
options: Comparing to competitors
Finding new prospects who resemble customers
Aligning the message to each segment
Turning a customer list into a reachable audience
quiz.why: Turning the list into a reachable audience.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business that keeps no customer records
A brand-new business with no customers yet
A veterinary clinic, because clients drift rather than leave
A client who only wants strangers
quiz.why: Lapsed customers drift — bring them back.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: A lower cost per thousand than prospecting
Reaching people who already bought, everywhere they go
Guaranteed repeat purchases
A report of which customers saw the ad
quiz.why: Reaching known buyers everywhere they go.

quiz.text: A client worries their customers will know the list was shared. What do you say?
options: The list matches devices — nothing about a customer is displayed
Customers never find out about targeting
The data is fully anonymised before upload
Use a smaller portion of the list to reduce risk
quiz.why: The list matches devices; nothing is displayed.

quiz.text: What should you agree at the first meeting?
options: That email stops
That only the last twelve months are included
That the list gets refreshed periodically
That it's reviewed against email monthly
quiz.why: A decaying list needs periodic refresh.

quiz.text: How are the households chosen?
options: A radius around the business
The client supplies a list, or we build one to their description
From people who visited the client's website
A purchased list of everybody in the trading area
quiz.why: Supply a list, or we build one to description.

quiz.text: Who inside the household gets reached?
options: The named resident
The primary decision maker from the data provider
Everybody in the home, on their screens
Whoever uses the internet most
quiz.why: Everybody in the home, on their screens.

quiz.text: What is the third mechanic mostly about?
options: Adding more households
Matching creative to each household
Measuring how many households responded
Reducing waste and keeping the list current
quiz.why: Reducing waste and keeping the list current.

quiz.text: “Household-level targeting” means the ad goes to…
options: Devices at that address
One named individual per address
The whole street
Anybody who visited that location
quiz.why: Devices at that address.

quiz.text: A “curated list” is…
options: Their best customers
Addresses verified against postal records
A list built to the client's description
Households ranked by likelihood to respond
quiz.why: A list built to the client's description.

quiz.text: A “first-party address list” comes from…
options: A licensed consumer data provider
The client's own records
Public records
Website or social engagement
quiz.why: The client's own records.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: Customers spread evenly across a state
A client needing one named individual
A seller of low-cost impulse items
An HVAC company, because a furnace is decided by the household
quiz.why: A household decision — reach everybody in it.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Almost no waste, and the whole household included
The cheapest option
Guaranteed delivery to every household
A record of which households saw the ad
quiz.why: Almost no waste — and the whole household.

quiz.text: A client says they don't have a list of addresses. What do you say?
options: A list can be purchased at extra cost
Suggest they collect addresses and revisit
You don't need one — describe your customer and we'll build it
Recommend geofencing instead for now
quiz.why: You don't need a list — we build it.

quiz.text: What should you build into the relationship at the first meeting?
options: A quarterly review
A monthly increase in household count
The client verifying each address personally
A periodic list refresh, because households move
quiz.why: Households move — refresh the list.

quiz.text: What does “build the audience” involve?
options: Growing the follower count first
Increasing post frequency
Defining who should see the ad — beyond current followers
Choosing which existing posts to fund
quiz.why: Define who sees it, beyond current followers.

quiz.text: “Pick the format” is about…
options: Selecting the ad type that fits the goal and creative
Choosing the platform
Deciding mobile versus desktop
Setting the creative's dimensions
quiz.why: The ad type that fits the goal and creative.

quiz.text: Why does this need weekly management?
options: Platform rules change constantly
The client expects a call
Reports are generated by hand each week
Creative tires and audiences fade, so budget has to move
quiz.why: Creative tires — budget has to move.

quiz.text: The difference between a boosted post and an ad campaign is…
options: Boosting is free
Boosted posts reach existing followers; ads build audiences
Boosted posts run longer
Ads need agency platform access
quiz.why: Boosting talks to followers; ads build reach.

quiz.text: An “ad set” is…
options: The finished creative
The best-performing organic posts
All the ads running in a month
The audience, budget, and placement grouping in a campaign
quiz.why: Audience, budget, and placement grouping.

quiz.text: A “call to action” is…
options: The ad's headline
A phone number at the end
The instruction telling somebody what to do next
Where the brand name first appears
quiz.why: The instruction for what to do next.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business with no visual material
A clothing boutique, because new arrivals give it something fresh
A client who only wants existing followers
A business that won't allow weekly management
quiz.why: Fresh things to show, week after week.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit over boosting?
options: It reaches people who don't already follow them
It costs less per person reached
It gets more comments and shares
It lets the client post more often
quiz.why: It reaches people who don't already follow.

quiz.text: A client says their nephew boosts posts and it's fine. What do you say?
options: Boosting is generally a waste of money
Offer to take over boosting cheaper
Tell them to stop posting and move all budget to ads
Boosting spends money on the audience they have; ads build a bigger one
quiz.why: Boosting and advertising are different jobs.

quiz.text: What should you settle at the first meeting?
options: That the client hands over the page password
What you're actually measuring
That the campaign runs at least six months
That we produce the creative
quiz.why: Set a measure that matters in month one.

quiz.text: “Build it like a post” means the creative…
options: Is written by the client's social manager
Gets published on the client's page first
Must be approved by the platform before launch
Uses the format and feel of a social post rather than a banner
quiz.why: It wears the format of a social post.

quiz.text: Where does the ad actually run?
options: Inside social feeds
On the open web — news, weather, recipes, apps
Only on mobile devices
On a list of sites the client approves
quiz.why: On the open web, not the social platforms.

quiz.text: “Keep it live” refers to…
options: Running the campaign without pausing
Refreshing the creative every fortnight
The social proof updating in real time while it runs
Keeping the client's pages active
quiz.why: Real likes and comments updating live.

quiz.text: A “social display ad” is best described as…
options: Social-style creative delivered across the open web
An ad inside a social platform
A boosted post
An ad made from a client's social content
quiz.why: Social-style creative, open-web delivery.

quiz.text: “Social proof” here means…
options: Proof the campaign ran
Testimonials the client provides
Evidence the client is active on social
The visible likes and comments on the ad itself
quiz.why: The visible likes and comments on the ad.

quiz.text: The “open web” means…
options: Websites with no paywall
Everywhere online outside the social platforms
Sites that accept programmatic ads
The publishers in the client's campaign
quiz.why: Everywhere online outside social.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A client who only wants to appear in social feeds
A business with no photography
A brewery, because its social content already travels well
A client judging purely on clicks
quiz.why: Content that already looks good and travels.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: A familiar look, in places social can't reach
Lower cost than social advertising
Guaranteed likes and shares on the page
Access to social platform targeting data
quiz.why: A familiar look, where social can't reach.

quiz.text: A client asks whether this runs on Facebook. What do you say?
options: Confirm it does, since the creative is social
It runs on Facebook and the open web at once
It depends which package they choose
No — it looks like a social post, but it runs everywhere else
quiz.why: Looks like a post; runs on the open web.

quiz.text: Besides the click pre-frame, what must be clear at the first meeting?
options: That creative is refreshed monthly
That social proof can't be guaranteed
Which product they're actually buying
That social ads are excluded
quiz.why: Be clear which product they bought.

quiz.text: Where does the creative come from?
options: Video the client already has, usually from social
A commercial produced for the campaign
A template the platform provides
Licensed commercial stock footage
quiz.why: Video the client already has.

quiz.text: What is the QR code for?
options: Tracking how many people watched
Verifying the ad played in full
Giving a television viewer a way to respond
Letting the client preview the ad
quiz.why: A way for a TV viewer to respond.

quiz.text: “Aim it like digital, not like TV” means…
options: Buying by daypart
Running only on mobile
Measuring against digital benchmarks
Choosing audiences and geography instead of programmes and time slots
quiz.why: Target audiences and geography, not slots.

quiz.text: “OTT” and “CTV” refer to…
options: Two competing ad formats
Streaming over the internet, and the TVs it plays on
Two pricing models for video
The two largest streaming platforms
quiz.why: Streaming, and the televisions it plays on.

quiz.text: “Co-viewing” means…
options: More than one person watching the same screen
Watching on two devices at once
The same ad on several services
Subscribing to multiple platforms
quiz.why: More than one person on the same screen.

quiz.text: “Non-skippable” means…
options: The ad can't be muted
The ad repeats until engagement
The whole ad plays
It can't be removed
quiz.why: The whole ad plays through.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A client with a polished thirty-second commercial
A business with no video anywhere
A client who wants specific programmes and dayparts
A martial arts school, because its social video is genuinely good
quiz.why: Good social video, no commercial — sell this.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: A lower cost than the streaming TV product
Television reach without producing a commercial
Guaranteed placement in premium programming
Access to social audience data
quiz.why: TV reach without producing a commercial.

quiz.text: A client asks whether this is a social media ad. What do you say?
options: Yes — creative and delivery both come from social
It runs on social and connected TVs at once
No — social describes the creative; this plays on the television
The distinction doesn't matter in practice
quiz.why: Social is the creative; it plays on TV.

quiz.text: What must be settled before the first invoice?
options: Which product they're buying
Whether a QR code is used
How long the campaign runs
Who owns the social video
quiz.why: Which product they're buying, in writing.

quiz.text: How many campaigns does this run as?
options: One per targeting method
One campaign, on one device, using several methods together
Two — one prospecting, one retargeting
One per geographic area
quiz.why: One campaign, one device, several methods.

quiz.text: Why do the methods work better stacked?
options: The platform charges less combined
Stacking increases total impressions
Combined reporting is simpler
The same phone gets reached more than one way
quiz.why: The same phone reached more than one way.

quiz.text: The third mechanic is about…
options: Adding more methods over time
Choosing which method to prioritise
Managing it weekly and measuring what it produced
Expanding onto tablets and desktop
quiz.why: Weekly management and measurement.

quiz.text: “Purchase intent” targeting reaches people based on…
options: Signals suggesting they're in the market for something
Their income bracket
Products they already bought from the client
Categories they follow on social
quiz.why: Signals that they're in the market.

quiz.text: “Store retargeting” builds an audience from…
options: People who clicked the ad
Devices that visited the client's own location
The client's mailing list
Households near the business
quiz.why: Devices that visited the client's location.

quiz.text: “Ad retargeting” reaches…
options: Anybody in the target area
Customers who bought after seeing the ad
Devices that entered a competitor recently
People who already saw the ad or visited the site
quiz.why: People who already saw the ad or the site.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A coffee drive-thru, because its customers decide on the move
A business whose customers are never on their phones
A client already buying geofencing and display separately
A business that only wants desktop
quiz.why: Customers deciding on the move, phone in hand.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: The lowest cost per thousand
Guaranteed store visits each month
Reaching somebody across their whole day, on the screen they carry
A list of every device that passed by
quiz.why: The phone follows them all day.

quiz.text: A client asks if this duplicates their geofencing. What do you say?
options: Reassure them the products are entirely separate
Geofencing is one of the methods inside this — check what they already buy
Duplication improves performance
Cancel the standalone geofencing immediately
quiz.why: Geofencing is inside this — check overlap.

quiz.text: What should be confirmed in writing before the order?
options: The exact number of devices reached
Which of the four methods performs best
That store retargeting is free
What they already buy, so nobody pays twice
quiz.why: Confirm overlap so nobody pays twice.

quiz.text: What does one buy give you access to?
options: A single streaming service
The client's choice of two platforms
A range of streaming audio and podcast services at once
Every service, including ad-free tiers
quiz.why: A range of audio and podcast services at once.

quiz.text: “Buy the listener, not the station” means…
options: Choosing programmes instead of times
Targeting people by who and where they are, not by service
Buying only the largest platform
Picking individual podcast episodes
quiz.why: Target the person, not the service.

quiz.text: The third mechanic covers…
options: Reporting and attribution
How the budget splits between services
Which voice talent records the ad
The spot itself and the moment it lands in
quiz.why: The spot and the moment it lands in.

quiz.text: “Digital audio” includes…
options: Streaming music and podcasts
Only broadcast radio streamed online
Any audio on a phone
Podcasts only
quiz.why: Streaming music and podcasts.

quiz.text: “Time-of-day targeting” lets you…
options: Choose which podcasts to appear in
Limit how often somebody hears the ad
Reach people during specific parts of the day
Schedule around the client's opening hours
quiz.why: Reach people at specific parts of the day.

quiz.text: The difference between host-read and inserted is…
options: Host-read is voiced by the presenter; inserted is your spot dropped in
Length
Host-read costs far less to produce
Inserted ads only run in music streaming
quiz.why: Host-read is the presenter; inserted is your spot.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business whose customers only consume visual media
A client who needs a click to judge it
A business with no audio and no budget to make any
An HVAC company, because its customers are driving between jobs
quiz.why: Customers with ears free but no screen.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: The cheapest cost per thousand
Reaching people in the hours no screen can
Guaranteed host endorsement
A list of every listener
quiz.why: It reaches the screen-free hours.

quiz.text: A client says digital audio is for young people. What do you say?
options: Agree, and recommend a different tactic
Age data isn't available for audio
That was true five years ago — the fastest growth is now people over fifty-five
Suggest testing it for a month to find out
quiz.why: The fastest growth is the over-fifty-fives.

quiz.text: What should you settle at the first meeting?
options: What you're measuring, because there is no click
Whether the client supplies a host-read script
Which services to exclude
That the creative comes in three lengths
quiz.why: No click — agree the measure up front.

quiz.text: What are the three placements?
options: Mobile, desktop, and tablet
Skippable, non-skippable, and bumper
Feed, story, and in-stream
Pre-roll, mid-roll, and post-roll
quiz.why: Pre-roll, mid-roll, and post-roll.

quiz.text: Where does this video play?
options: On connected televisions
Inside social media feeds
Around video content on websites and apps
On streaming services with premium programming
quiz.why: Around video on websites and apps.

quiz.text: The creative rules matter most because…
options: The first few seconds are the only guaranteed ones
Platforms reject non-compliant creative
Video files must meet strict specs
Brand guidelines must be applied consistently
quiz.why: Only the first few seconds are guaranteed.

quiz.text: “Pre-roll” plays…
options: After the content ends
Before the content the person chose
Partway through longer videos
Between two unrelated pieces
quiz.why: Before the content the viewer chose.

quiz.text: “In-stream” means the ad appears…
options: Beside the video player
As a banner over the picture
In a separate window that opens automatically
Within the video content itself
quiz.why: Within the video content itself.

quiz.text: “Cross-device” means…
options: The ad works on any screen size
The same person can be reached on their other screens
The creative is delivered in several formats
It runs on mobile and desktop at once
quiz.why: The same person, reached on other screens.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A client whose only video puts the logo at the very end
A business that wants to be on television
A technical college, because its audience watches how-to content
A client with no video and no interest in making any
quiz.why: An audience that chooses to watch video.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Attention from somebody who chose to watch something
The lowest cost per completed view
Guaranteed full completion
Guaranteed placement by premium TV programming
quiz.why: Attention from a viewer who chose to watch.

quiz.text: A client says everybody skips video ads. What do you say?
options: Skip rates are lower than people believe
Skipping still counts as an impression
Recommend non-skippable formats elsewhere
Some do — and the first few seconds always play, which is why creative matters
quiz.why: The first few seconds always play.

quiz.text: What should be agreed about the creative?
options: That we shoot a new video
That the spot runs no longer than fifteen seconds
The message comes first and the logo comes early
That we add captions in production
quiz.why: Message first, logo early.

quiz.text: “Wear the page's clothes” means the ad…
options: Matches the look and format of the site it appears on
Uses the client's brand colours
Is written by the publication's editorial staff
Appears only on industry-relevant sites
quiz.why: It matches the look of the host page.

quiz.text: How is the click earned?
options: With a discount offer
By placing the ad at the top of the page
Through a call to action repeated in the creative
With a headline that promises something worth reading
quiz.why: A headline worth reading earns the click.

quiz.text: What has to happen on the other side of the click?
options: A form loads
The page delivers what the headline promised
The visitor is added to a retargeting audience
The client's contact details appear prominently
quiz.why: The page must deliver the headline's promise.

quiz.text: The “sponsored label” is…
options: Optional but recommended
Added by the publisher at their discretion
Required, and it helps rather than hurts
Applied only when the advertiser requests it
quiz.why: Required — and it builds trust.

quiz.text: A “content-first headline” does what?
options: Offers something useful rather than selling
Names the business immediately
Poses a question the article answers
Includes the primary keyword for search
quiz.why: It offers something useful, not a pitch.

quiz.text: “Qualified traffic” means…
options: More clicks
Visitors from a relevant publication
Traffic verified as non-automated
Fewer clicks from more interested people
quiz.why: Fewer clicks, from more interested people.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A client who wants the highest click volume
A family jeweller, because buying advice earns attention
A business with nothing to explain
A client who won't allow a sponsored label
quiz.why: Something worth explaining earns the read.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Cheaper clicks than display
Guaranteed editorial placement
Being useful before asking for anything
Higher click volume than banners
quiz.why: Being useful before asking for anything.

quiz.text: A client says they've nothing to write about. What do you ask?
options: What customers always ask that they get wrong
Whether they have a blog already
Whether they'd like our team to write it
What competitors are publishing this quarter
quiz.why: Their most-asked question is the article.

quiz.text: What must be agreed up front about measurement?
options: Reporting will be delivered weekly
The article will be refreshed each quarter
That clicks will match banners
Fewer clicks, better clicks
quiz.why: Judge it on quality, not click volume.

quiz.text: What is true of the four ad formats?
options: They all allow the viewer to skip after five seconds have elapsed
They are all priced identically on a cost-per-view basis
Each one has a different length limit and a different clock
Only two of them are available to local advertisers
quiz.why: Four formats, four clocks.

quiz.text: “Choose the content, not just the audience” means you can…
options: Name the channels and topics your ad plays in front of
Select which demographic groups are shown the advertisement
Pick the time of day
Decide how many times each viewer will see the advertisement
quiz.why: The content itself, not just who sees it.

quiz.text: What is the five-second rule?
options: Ads must run five seconds
Viewers who watch five seconds are billed as a completed view
Creative must be refreshed every five weeks to avoid fatigue
Everything essential happens before the skip button appears
quiz.why: Name and point up front.

quiz.text: A “bumper ad” is…
options: A fifteen-second non-skippable spot
Six seconds, non-skippable
An end-of-video ad
A short ad that appears as an overlay on the video player
quiz.why: Six seconds, can’t be skipped.

quiz.text: “Channel targeting” lets an advertiser…
options: Choose which streaming service the ad appears on
Choose a network
Limit the campaign to channels above a set subscriber count
Pick the specific channels their ad runs before
quiz.why: The most distinctive thing about YouTube.

quiz.text: “Outstream” refers to ads that run…
options: Outside the client’s chosen geography
After the main content has finished playing entirely
On partner sites and apps, not on YouTube itself
Without sound unless the viewer chooses to unmute them
quiz.why: Partner network, mobile and tablet only.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A client whose only piece of video saves the business name right until the very end
A paint store, because people watch how-to videos before starting
A business whose customers never watch online video of any kind
A client who wants to buy the local evening news
quiz.why: Their customer is already watching how-to videos.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Choosing the exact videos your ad appears before
A lower cost per view than television advertising
Guaranteed completion of every advertisement served
The live channel audience
quiz.why: Nothing else lets you pick the content.

quiz.text: A client says their customers are too old for YouTube. What do you ask?
options: Whether they have taken a proper look at their own website analytics recently
Whether they would consider a smaller test budget to find out
What age range they believe their customers actually fall into
When their furnace went out, did they watch a video about it first
quiz.why: The furnace question makes your point for you.

quiz.text: What should be agreed about the creative?
options: That a new commercial will be produced before launch
The first five seconds carry the message
That the video will run no longer than fifteen seconds
That captions are added
quiz.why: Settle it before production.

quiz.text: Where does this advertisement run?
options: On websites and apps around video content
Within social feeds on connected devices
On the YouTube platform alongside creator content
Inside streaming services, on the television
quiz.why: Inside the services, on the big screen.

quiz.text: What are the three ways it can be aimed?
options: By daypart, by programme, and by network
Geography, audience, and what’s actually on the screen
By household income, by age bracket, and by geography, and nothing else besides
By channel, by genre, and by time of day
quiz.why: Geography, audience, and the screen itself.

quiz.text: How should it be measured?
options: By click-through rate on the advertisement
By the number of impressions delivered each month
By what happens afterwards — traffic, searches, and calls
By setting the results side by side against the client’s existing cable schedule
quiz.why: There’s no click on a television.

quiz.text: “OTT” and “CTV” describe…
options: Streaming over the internet, and the televisions it plays on
Two competing streaming platforms
Two different ways of pricing streaming inventory
The two largest streaming services currently available to local advertisers
quiz.why: Over-the-top delivery; connected televisions.

quiz.text: “ACR” allows targeting based on…
options: Browsing history
The channels a household previously subscribed to
Recognition of which household member is watching
What is actually on the television screen
quiz.why: The set reports what’s on screen — aggregated.

quiz.text: A “cord-cutter” is somebody who…
options: Has never had a television subscription
Watches television only on mobile devices
Cancelled cable or satellite
Has several streaming services
quiz.why: They cancelled — and still watch television.

quiz.text: Which is the strongest fit?
options: A business that only ever serves customers within one small neighbourhood
A furniture store, because it’s a considered purchase decided at home
A client who needs a click to judge whether it worked
A business with no video creative and no plan to make any
quiz.why: Considered purchases decided in the living room.

quiz.text: What is the core benefit?
options: Television reach without paying for geography they don’t serve
A lower cost per thousand than cable advertising
Guaranteed placement in the local evening news
A complete household-by-household list of everyone who saw the advertisement
quiz.why: Television, without the waste.

quiz.text: A client says they already buy cable. What do you say?
options: Recommend they cancel the cable buy and move the budget across
Say the audiences overlap
Suggest running both and comparing the results after ninety days
Cable reaches the people who still have cable
quiz.why: The sentence that lands.

quiz.text: What should you settle at the first meeting?
options: That the campaign runs for a minimum of six months
Which programmes it runs in
What success looks like, because there’s no click
That a new commercial will be produced before launch
quiz.why: Agree the measure before it runs.

quiz.text: What does an advertiser choose first?
options: The channels and the geography
The programme
The demographic profile of the household
The daypart and the frequency of the schedule
quiz.why: Channels and geography come first.

quiz.text: What does the second mechanic allow?
options: Increasing the budget partway through a flight
Switching channels once the campaign has launched
Narrowing the audience further, if it’s worth doing
Adding a second geographic area without having to change anything about the buy
quiz.why: Narrow further only if it’s worth doing.

quiz.text: Why include a QR code?
options: To measure how many households saw the advertisement
To verify the advertisement played in full
To let the client preview the finished spot before launch
